19.1 i ntroduction
When testing hypotheses concerning the means of two populations, thus far we have used
independent samples; the values in the first sample have no effect on those in the second.
Suppose, however, that we wish to assess the effectiveness of a training program by com-
paring pretraining test scores for a single group of people. An individual who scored well
before the training could also be expected to score well after; the two samples are dependent,
and rather than examine the two samples separately, we use as our sample matched-pairs
of values the pairs of scores for each individual in the experiment. In this chapter, we will
consider matched-pair hypothesis tests for the difference of two means and t-Tests for the
difference in population proportions.
Samples of matched-pairs occur in two situations. In the first, of which the experiment
described above is an example, measurements are made on the elements of a single sam-
ple group before and after the application of an experimental treatment, or after each of
two different treatments. In the second, members of two groups are paired, and different
treatments applied to the two groups. In a study of the effects of smoking on the inci-
dence of heart disease, individuals might be matched by such characteristics as age, sex,
weight, occupation, diet, family medical history, and environment, but with one member
of each pair a smoker. Differences between members of a pair in subsequent medical
history can then be more reasonably ascribed to smoking, since other factors were made
identical.

20.1 i ntroduction
Confidence intervals can be used as an alternative for hypothesis testing in business decision
making. A hypothesis test is usually a yes-no decision. We either reject a hypothesis or fail
to reject it. A confidence interval not only gives that answer, but it also provides information
about the possible range of values for the parameter.
Confidence intervals are in general easier to understand and explain to decision makers than
hypothesis tests. In this chapter, we will review hypothesis testing situations and resolve
those situations with confidence intervals.
20.2 c hoosing a c onfidence Level
Often we have used confidence levels of 90% or 95% in our illustrations and examples. In
reality, these confidence levels are not the only values used. The choice of the confidence
level is based on the loss one would sustain if the parameter is outside the range and the gain
one would have if the parameter is inside the range. If the loss is high compared to the gain,
the confidence levels should be high. If the loss is negligible compared to the gain, a lower
confidence level is fine.
In general, one must be cautious when interpreting confidence levels. When reviewing a
research article with a 60% confidence level, do not make the assumption that the confi-
dence is low and conclude that it is not worthy of making a decision based upon the underly-
ing parameter. Even if the parameter is significant at the 99% confidence level, it is possible
for decision makers to say that the confidence level is not high enough if the loss due to
wrong decisions is large.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 20.3 Hypothesis t esting versus c onfidence i ntervals
chunks.sectionTitle: Hypothesis t esting versus c onfidence i ntervals
chunks.content:
20.3 Hypothesis t esting versus c onfidence i ntervals
Rather than just a simple yes-no decision, as encountered with hypothesis tests, confidence
intervals also provide the possible range of values for the parameter. A narrow confidence
interval indicates that the parameter has been estimated with a high degree of precision.
Wide confidence intervals indicate that a low precision is involved in the yes-no decision
making. Decision makers often need to know the precision rather than or in addition to the
simple yes-no answers in testing. When testing the null hypothesis that the means from two
samples are the same and we have a [–50, 50] confidence interval for the difference in the
population means, we can state there is no difference between the means since the interval
includes zero. But think how much stronger the result would be if the confidence interval
was [–1, 1].
Management is usually more receptive to confidence intervals since they are visual, making
them easier to understand and communicate. Clearly it would be easier to comprehend that
a parameter is in a specific range than to know that the probability of the parameter being
one specific value is less than a specified percentage.
